blocks.text: .3 Governance in Light of the Qur’an

segments.text: This topic asks for normative principles drawn from Qur’anic guidance, and how they relate to public authority, justice, and collective responsibility — with the syllabus’s explicit caution against making
unsupported claims about a single, fixed Qur’anic “administrative model.”

The Qur’an establishes normative principles (justice, trust, accountability) rather than a single specified administrative blueprint, and an answer claiming otherwise would overstate what the primary source actually specifies, conflating normative principle with a particular historical or scholarly interpretation of institutional design.

blocks.text: .4 Governance in Light of the Sunnah

items.text: This unit’s four sub-topics move from broad Qur’anic principles to the Prophetic Sunnah to the more elaborated juristic reasoning of Fiqh — each successive source adding interpretive and practical detail to the principles established at the Qur’anic level.

The unit’s repeated, non-negotiable methodological standard — verified sources only, no invented quotations or references, explicit acknowledgment of genuine scholarly diversity — is itself as much a tested skill in this unit as the substantive content of the principles themselves.

The core principles here (justice, trust, consultation, accountability, welfare, rule-bound authority, equality before law) map closely onto the secular good-governance characteristics from Unit I — a genuinely useful comparative observation for an answer connecting the two units.
